Dear Pinecrest Insights Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the new-grad Data Analyst role starting summer 2027. I'm a Computer Science senior at Brookfield University with a minor in Data Science, graduating in May 2027. My work so far has split between building dashboards for a product team and doing qualitative research on young people's online lives. Your role uses both, which is a big part of why it appeals to me.

This past summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company. I built a Tableau dashboard that the product team used to track weekly active students, lessons completed, and streaks. I also wrote the SQL tables behind it. Early on I found that sessions were being double-counted whenever students put the app in the background. I fixed this by redefining a session as activity with gaps under 30 minutes, using window functions over the event timestamps. After that the weekly numbers matched how students actually used the app. My manager found the streak breakdown by grade level especially useful. That project taught me that a dashboard is only as trustworthy as the tables underneath it.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in Brookfield's Social Computing Lab. I support a PhD student's interview study on how teens aged 15–17 use online communities for mental-health support. I sent recruitment messages and ran the eligibility screener. I also transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, replacing names, schools, and community names with placeholders. Later I coded six transcripts using the team's codebook. In our inter-rater reliability check we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of reconciliation. Working with this data taught me to be careful with sensitive information about young people. It also taught me to write down my reasoning when my judgment differs from a colleague's. I'd bring both habits to coding open-ended survey responses and supporting stakeholder interviews at Pinecrest.

I'm most interested in the moments when the numbers and the people don't line up. In a machine learning course project, my team of three fine-tuned a small transformer to classify the sentiment of Reddit support posts. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. My part was the error analysis. I found that the model often labeled sarcastic or dark-humor posts as negative, which is a reminder that people don't always say what they mean in the way a model expects. That's the kind of question I'd like to help your education, healthcare, and nonprofit clients answer.

I'd welcome the chance to learn from your mentors, rotate across client domains, and practice presenting findings directly to clients. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
Avery Santos

---

The Fieldstone letter said you "managed" the lab study and "developed" the classifier. Here I described those as supporting the PhD student's study and as a team project where you did the error analysis. That's more accurate and still reads strong. I left the PhD application out of this letter.

I didn't want to guess where your PhD interests are. Your notes say you don't have a research question yet and aren't sure whether you like the lab's topic or mostly like working with J. Kim. So this draft builds on a thread that does show up in your work: the gap between what a system measures and what people actually mean. I've marked the parts only you can fill in with **[brackets]**.

---

**Statement of Purpose — PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

In a machine learning course last fall, my team fine-tuned a small transformer to classify the sentiment of posts from Reddit mental-health support communities. The model beat our baseline, with a macro-F1 of 0.81 against 0.72. But the part I kept thinking about came after, when I did the error analysis. The model often labeled sarcastic or dark-humor posts as negative. Some of those posts were people joking about how bad their week had been. Others were people saying something serious in a way that only sounded like a joke. To the model, they all looked the same. I want to study the moment when a system reads people one way and they mean something else, especially in online spaces where young people go for support. That question is why I'm applying to the HCI PhD program at Khoury.

I came to this question from two directions. Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab at Brookfield University, working with Prof. A. Moreno and PhD student J. Kim. J. Kim leads an interview study on how teens aged 15–17 use online communities for mental-health support. My role was supporting, not leading. I sent recruitment messages to community moderators and ran the eligibility screener. I transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews. Then I coded six transcripts with the team's codebook. In our inter-rater reliability check with J. Kim we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of reconciliation. The paper is now under review, and I'm listed in the acknowledgments.

Those tasks taught me more than I expected. De-identifying transcripts meant deciding, line by line, what could identify a teenager: a school name, a server name, a username. It made me take seriously how much these young people trusted the study. Coding taught me that disagreement is data. When J. Kim and I coded the same passage differently, writing memos to explain our reasoning often showed that the passage was ambiguous in a way the codebook hadn't anticipated. **[Optional: one or two sentences, in your own words, about what reading and listening to these interviews meant to you. Leave out any participant details.]**

The second direction was industry. Last summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company, where I built a Tableau dashboard of weekly student engagement. Early on, I found that sessions were being double-counted whenever students put the app in the background. Fixing that meant deciding what a "session" really is, and I chose activity with gaps under 30 minutes. It was a small decision, but the whole dashboard depended on it. The product team cared most about streaks, and I started wondering what a streak means to a student. Does it mean the student is learning, or that they're anxious about losing the streak? The dashboard couldn't tell us.

Together, these experiences point toward a question I want to explore in a PhD. Communities that support teens increasingly depend on automated tools: sentiment and toxicity classifiers, content moderation, engagement metrics. How do these tools interpret the ways teens actually talk about distress, such as humor, irony, and understatement? And what happens when they get it wrong? Possible projects include interview studies with teen community members and moderators about how they signal seriousness, error analyses of moderation models on support-community language, and design work on tools that leave room for that ambiguity instead of resolving it automatically. **[Edit or replace this paragraph. It's my synthesis of your experiences, not something you've told me you want to study.]**

I'm honest about where I am. I haven't led a study yet, and my research question is still forming. But I've seen the full lifecycle of a qualitative study up close, from recruitment through coding, and I know what careful, ethical work with young participants requires. On the computational side, I can build models and pipelines and, maybe more importantly, take them apart to see where they fail. A PhD is where I want to learn to put those together and lead the work myself.

Khoury is a strong fit because **[name 1–3 faculty whose work you've actually read, and say specifically why: a paper, a method, a population. I haven't verified current faculty, so please check the program page.]** I'm also drawn to **[a lab, center, or interdisciplinary connection at Northeastern that matters to you]**.

After the PhD, I hope to **[academia / industry research / policy or nonprofit work: your call]**. Wherever I end up, I want to keep asking what our systems miss about the people they're built to serve.

---

Questions before you finalize this:

1. **Does the research direction feel like yours?** I connected your sarcasm error analysis, the lab's moderation and peer-support agenda, and the streak question. If none of it excites you, that tells us something, and it's better to find out now than in an interview.
2. **Which Khoury faculty?** If you'd like, I can look up current HCI faculty for you to read up on. Naming someone whose work you haven't read is risky.
3. **Prompt and length.** Check the program's exact prompt and page or word limit. Many programs ask for 1–2 pages, and this draft runs about 850 words.
4. **Letter alignment.** You were worried that Prof. Moreno doesn't know you well. It's worth sending them and J. Kim this statement along with a short list of what you did, so the letter backs up the same story.

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. We posit that LLM privacy must be understood as a lifecycle-wide problem, rather than being reduced to training-data leakage alone. We introduce a taxonomy of five open privacy problems posed by LLMs and flesh out each with concrete threat models, real-world case studies, and open research challenges. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,772 AI/ML privacy papers from leading conferences (2016–2025), we reveal a disproportionate research focus: memorization dominates technical research, yet offers little traction against pressing problems like inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent behavior, and surveillance-enabling data aggregation. We provide a roadmap of technical, sociotechnical, and policy interventions, and call on the community to prioritize the underexplored problem categories—agent-based leakage, inference attacks, and data aggregation—that collectively receive less than 9% of current research attention.

CIDER: A Dataset of Contextual Disclosure Boundaries for Privacy Preference Alignment

Bingcan Guo, Eryue Xu, Jijie Zhou, Zhiping Zhang, and  Tianshi Li

In COLM 2026 Oct 2026

Abs arXiv Dataset Code

Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human privacy preferences requires capturing individuals’ disclosure boundaries beyond general privacy norms. However, current models lack methods for eliciting such nuanced preferences and ground truth data to evaluate alignment in realistic settings. We introduce CIDER, a dataset of 14,850 human annotations from 169 users, forming 1,650 contextual disclosure boundary sets across 60 interpersonal communication scenarios where information sharing violates privacy norms. Each boundary represents a real user’s disclosure decisions over 9 sharing variants, given a communication role and AI-mediated condition. We formulate a prediction task in which models predict a user’s disclosure decision from historical boundaries, with varying levels of contextual information. Across eight open and proprietary models, personalization improves performance, with accuracy gains of up to 11.41% using six in-context examples. However, these gains arise from different mechanisms. Larger models such as GPT-5.4 (with medium reasoning effort) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 leverage semantic context to infer user-specific, context-dependent disclosure preferences for more accurate predictions, while smaller models tend to rely on structured heuristics based on disclosure granularity and identifiability and present trade-offs between false positives and false negatives. Our findings highlight the potential and limitations of current LLMs’ privacy modeling capability and position CIDER as a resource for advancing personalized privacy preference alignment.

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, and  Tianshi Li

In COLM 2026 Oct 2026

Abs arXiv

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users’ behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization’s effects on users’ privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, through improving users’ perceived control, attenuates personalization’s adverse effects by reducing the increase in privacy concerns and the decrease in trust. Our results suggest that designing agent’s autonomy that supports human autonomy (both in terms of perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns, contributing to the development of trustworthy LLM agents.

PrivacyMotiv: Speculative Persona Journeys for Empathic and Motivating Privacy Reviews in UX Design

Zeya Chen, Jianing Wen, Yaxing Yao, Toby Jia-Jun Li, and  Tianshi Li

In DIS 2026 Jun 2026

Abs arXiv Demo

UX professionals routinely conduct design reviews, yet privacy concerns are often overlooked—not only due to limited tools, but more fundamentally from low intrinsic motivation, driven by limited privacy knowledge, weak empathy for unexpectedly affected users, and low confidence in identifying harms. We present PrivacyMotiv, an LLM-powered system that supports privacy-oriented design diagnosis by generating speculative personas with UX user journeys centered on individuals vulnerable to privacy risks. Drawing on narrative strategies, the system constructs relatable and attention-drawing scenarios that show how ordinary design choices may cause unintended harms, expanding the scope of privacy reflection in UX. In a within-subjects study with professional UX practitioners (N=16), we compared participants’ self-proposed methods with PrivacyMotiv across two privacy audit tasks. Results show significant improvements in empathy, intrinsic motivation, and perceived usefulness. This work contributes empirical insight into motivational barriers in privacy-aware UX and a novel mechanism for structured privacy audits.

Operationalizing Data Minimization for Privacy-Preserving LLM Prompting

Jijie Zhou, Niloofar Mireshghallah, and  Tianshi Li

In ICLR 2026 Apr 2026

Abs arXiv Code Website

The rapid deployment of large language models (LLMs) in consumer applications has led to frequent exchanges of personal information. To obtain useful responses, users often share more than necessary, increasing privacy risks via memorization, context-based personalization, or security breaches. We present a framework to formally define and operationalize data minimization: for a given user prompt and response model, quantifying the least privacy-revealing disclosure that maintains utility, and propose a priority-queue tree search to locate this optimal point within a privacy-ordered transformation space. We evaluated the framework on four datasets spanning open-ended conversations (ShareGPT, WildChat) and knowledge-intensive tasks with single-ground-truth answers (CaseHOLD, MedQA), quantifying achievable data minimization with nine LLMs as the response model. Our results demonstrate that larger frontier LLMs can tolerate stronger data minimization while maintaining task quality than smaller open-source models (85.7% redaction for GPT-5 vs. 19.3% for Qwen2.5-0.5B). By comparing with our search-derived benchmarks, we find that LLMs struggle to predict optimal data minimization directly, showing a bias toward abstraction that leads to oversharing. This suggests not just a privacy gap, but a capability gap: models may lack awareness of what information they actually need to solve a task.

Eryue Xu, and  Tianshi Li

In CHI 2026 Apr 2026

Managing one’s digital footprint is overwhelming, as it spans multiple platforms and involves countless context-dependent decisions. Recent advances in agentic AI offer ways forward by enabling holistic, contextual privacy-enhancing solutions. Building on this potential, we adopted a “human-as-the-unit” perspective and investigated users’ cross-context privacy challenges through 12 semi-structured interviews. Results reveal that people rely on ad hoc manual strategies while lacking comprehensive privacy controls, highlighting nine privacy-management challenges across applications, temporal contexts, and relationships. The three highest-ranked concepts were all post-sharing management tools with half or full agent autonomy, with users expressing greater trust in AI accuracy than in their own efforts. In CSCW 2025 Oct 2025

The advancements of Large Language Models (LLMs) have decentralized the responsibility for the transparency of AI usage. Specifically, LLM users are now encouraged or required to disclose the use of LLM-generated content for varied types of real-world tasks. However, an emerging phenomenon, users’ secret use of LLMs, raises challenges in ensuring end users adhere to the transparency requirement. Our study used mixed-methods with an exploratory survey (125 real-world secret use cases reported) and a controlled experiment among 300 users to investigate the contexts and causes behind the secret use of LLMs. We found that such secretive behavior is often triggered by certain tasks, transcending demographic and personality differences among users. The proliferation of LLM-based conversational agents has resulted in excessive disclosure of identifiable or sensitive information. The emergence of large-language models (LLMs), and their increased use in user-facing systems, has led to substantial privacy concerns. Zhiping Zhang, Michelle Jia, Hao-Ping (Hank) Lee, Bingsheng Yao, Sauvik Das, Ada Lerner, Dakuo Wang, and  Tianshi Li

In CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems Apr 2024

The widespread use of Large Language Model (LLM)-based conversational agents (CAs), especially in high-stakes domains, raises many privacy concerns. Building ethical LLM-based CAs that respect user privacy requires an in-depth understanding of the privacy risks that concern users the most. However, existing research, primarily model-centered, does not provide insight into users’ perspectives. To bridge this gap, we analyzed sensitive disclosures in real-world ChatGPT conversations and conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 LLM-based CA users. We found that users are constantly faced with trade-offs between privacy, utility, and convenience when using LLM-based CAs. However, users’ erroneous mental models and the dark patterns in system design limited their awareness and comprehension of the privacy risks. Additionally, the human-like interactions encouraged more sensitive disclosures, which complicated users’ ability to navigate the trade-offs. We discuss practical design guidelines and the needs for paradigmatic shifts to protect the privacy of LLM-based CA users.

Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Technol. Apr 2024

Apple and Google introduced their versions of privacy nutrition labels to the mobile app stores to better inform users of the apps’ data practices. However, these labels are self-reported by developers and have been found to contain many inaccuracies due to misunderstandings of the label taxonomy. In this work, we present Matcha, an IDE plugin that uses automated code analysis to help developers create accurate Google Play data safety labels. Developers can benefit from Matcha’s ability to detect user data accesses and transmissions while staying in control of the generated label by adding custom Java annotations and modifying an auto-generated XML specification. Drawing on Matcha, we discuss general design recommendations for developer tools used to create accurate standardized privacy notices.

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

Biography

Tianshi Li is an assistant professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences at Northeastern University, based in Boston.

After obtaining her doctorate in human–computer interaction, Li joined UC Berkeley as a postdoctoral scholar, where she continued her research on usable privacy and security in mobile apps and explored novel privacy issues in human–LLM interactions. Li also worked at Google, where she applied her techniques to products that provide privacy compliance support to companies. Specifically, she developed a series of integrated development environment plugins to assist developers in building mobile apps with native privacy support by adding privacy annotations to their source code. Li is particularly interested in enabling developers who don’t specialize in privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness to create apps that still meet privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness requirements. She has published work at the CHI, IMWUT/UbiComp, CSCW, and PETS conferences, as well as the TOCHI journal, and has earned several “best paper” honors.

Li was drawn to Khoury College by the opportunity to pursue rich collaborative research in cybersecurity, privacy, and HCI. She is dedicated to developing practical techniques in that leverage technological advancements to address pressing societal issues. She also hopes to direct her own lab.

When she isn’t working, Li enjoys playing board games and the guitar.

**Statement of Purpose: PhD in Computer Science (Human-Computer Interaction), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

Last winter I was transcribing interviews for a study on how teens use online communities for mental-health support. One participant described a server that had been one of the few places they could say they were having a bad day. Then the moderators added an automated filter, and some of their posts quietly disappeared. They understood why the moderators had done it. Still, they described feeling silenced by a tool that was supposed to protect them. That interview has stayed with me, along with the question it raised: who are automated moderation tools actually for? And how do they change what young people feel safe saying when they're looking for help? I don't have a full answer, or even a finished research question. But I've found that this is the kind of problem I keep coming back to, and I'm applying to the HCI PhD program at Khoury to learn how to study it well.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab at Brookfield University, working with Prof. A. Moreno and PhD student J. Kim. J. Kim leads an interview study with 16 teens aged 15–17 about how they use online communities for mental-health support. My role was supporting, not leading. I sent recruitment messages to community moderators and ran the eligibility screener. I transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews. Then I coded six transcripts with the team's codebook. In our inter-rater reliability check with J. Kim we reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 after one round of reconciliation. The paper is now under review, and I'm listed in the acknowledgments.

The work taught me two things I'd want to build on. First, de-identification meant deciding, line by line, what could identify a teenager: a school, a username, the name of a server. I came away understanding how much trust participants placed in us, and how fragile anonymity can be. Second, coding taught me that disagreement is data. When J. Kim and I coded a passage differently, writing memos to explain our reasoning often showed that the passage was ambiguous in a way the codebook hadn't anticipated.

I'd seen a different side of the same problem a year earlier. In a machine learning course, my team of three fine-tuned a small transformer to classify the sentiment of posts from Reddit mental-health support communities. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, against 0.72 for our baseline. My part was the error analysis, and that was the part I found most interesting. The model often labeled sarcastic or dark-humor posts as negative. Some were people joking about a bad week. Others were people saying something serious in a way that only sounded like a joke. At the time it was just an accuracy problem. After the interview, I saw it differently. A moderation filter built on similar signals could remove the very posts where someone is reaching out in the only way they feel comfortable.

That's the direction I hope to explore. When teens know an automated system is watching, how do they decide what to say, how to phrase it, and whether to post at all? Do they soften their language, move to private messages, or leave? And how do moderators weigh protecting a community against making it a place where people can still say they're struggling? I'd like to approach these questions with interviews and qualitative analysis, which I've practiced, alongside computational methods, such as examining what moderation and sentiment models get wrong on support-community language. Eventually I'd like to explore design alternatives that give young people more agency over how their words are handled. I see this partly as a question about disclosure and privacy: when people share something vulnerable, they're making a judgment about who will see it and what will happen next. Automated moderation adds a new audience to that judgment.

I want to be honest about where I am. I haven't led a study, and I'm still figuring out exactly which question I want to own. What I bring is close experience with each stage of a qualitative study, an understanding of what careful work with young participants requires, and the technical skills to build models and then take them apart. A PhD is where I want to learn to combine these and lead the work myself.

I'm especially interested in working with Prof. Tianshi Li in the PEACH Lab. Prof. Li's framing of privacy as something that "sustains human agency, safe exploration, and free expression" describes what I think is at stake when a teen's post disappears. **[After reading, add one or two specifics. Strong candidates: "It's a Fair Game" (CHI '24), on how people weigh the risks and benefits of disclosing sensitive information to LLM chatbots; "Precarious But Active" (PETS 2026), on how members of fandom communities keep participating under censorship and surveillance; and the lab's work on re-identifying anonymized interview transcripts (AgentDoxx and the Anthropic Interviewer re-identification preprint), which connects directly to your de-identification work.]** I'd be excited to bring a focus on youth and online support communities to the lab's human-centered approach to privacy and AI. **[Optional: a second faculty member who works on online communities, moderation, or youth.]**

After the PhD, I hope to **[academia / industry research / nonprofit or policy work]**. Wherever I end up, I want to help build online spaces where young people can say they're having a bad day and be heard.
